guides.title: Greedy decisions and maximum-subarray state
guides.summary: Keep a proof of what can safely be forgotten.

sections.title: One stock trade: best buy so far
paragraphs: For each potential selling day, the best earlier buy is the lowest price seen so far. Keep that minimum and the largest observed sell-minus-buy difference. Updating the minimum first allows a zero-length “no profitable trade” candidate, which matches the at-most-one-trade contract.

The discarded prices cannot beat a cheaper earlier buy for a future sale. That dominance argument is the greedy proof. Empty or monotonically falling prices return zero. Widen arithmetic to long. Multiple trades, fees, cooldowns, or position constraints change the state and cannot be solved by blindly reusing this one-trade formula.

sections.title: Kadane’s algorithm is a small DP
paragraphs: Define endingHere as the best nonempty contiguous subarray ending at the current position. Either extend the previous subarray or start at the current element. Keep a separate global best because the optimal subarray may end before the last position.

Initialize from the first value rather than zero so all-negative input returns the largest negative value. Empty input is rejected under the nonempty contract. O(n) time, O(1) fixed-width extra space. This solves contiguous subarray sum, not arbitrary subsequence selection.
sections.example: [-4,-2,-7] returns -2, not 0; [4,-1,2] returns 5.

sections.title: Jump-game reachable frontier
paragraphs: Keep the farthest index reachable using positions already scanned. If the next index exceeds that frontier, no explored position can get you there, so the reachable region cannot expand further. Otherwise update the frontier with index+maximumJump.

This greedy summary answers reachability because reaching a position earlier does not consume a resource needed later. It does not automatically yield a minimum jump count or a path. Use long for index+jump and validate nonnegative jumps.

guides.title: Bit operations with narrow, useful contracts
guides.summary: Learn XOR cancellation and clear-lowest-bit before specialized bit tricks.

sections.title: XOR for one unpaired value
paragraphs: XOR is associative and commutative, x XOR x is zero, and x XOR zero is x. If every value occurs exactly twice except one, XORing the array cancels all paired values and leaves the singleton. No arithmetic overflow occurs because XOR acts on bits.

This contract is narrower than “find a unique value.” Values occurring three times or two separate singletons need different reasoning. The sample does not validate occurrence counts; that would require more work or memory. Empty input returns zero from the identity operation but does not satisfy the promised singleton contract. O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.title: Clear the lowest set bit
paragraphs: For a nonzero unsigned integer x, subtracting one flips the lowest one bit to zero and lower zeros to ones. x & (x-1) therefore clears exactly the lowest set bit. Repeat until zero to count set bits. A uint contract avoids confusing arithmetic right-shift behavior on negative signed numbers.

The loop runs once per set bit, at most 32 times for uint. A fixed-width built-in such as BitOperations.PopCount is preferable when permitted; understanding the invariant is still useful. C# shift counts are masked to the operand width, so shifting an int by 32 does not mean a 33-bit value. Do not use bitmask subset enumeration for large n without checking exponential output and width.

guides.title: C# queue, stack, deque, and heap APIs
guides.summary: Choose removal order first, then the collection.

sections.title: PriorityQueue is a min-heap
paragraphs: PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority> removes the element with the lowest priority under its comparer. Enqueue accepts payload and priority separately. Dequeue returns only the payload; TryDequeue also gives the priority and returns false if empty. Peek does not remove. Equal priorities are not guaranteed FIFO.

Heap insertion/removal costs O(log n), root access O(1). Enumeration is not sorted order. The complete example’s MinHeapRoot enqueues string payloads with integer priorities and verifies the earlier-priority item is removed first.

sections.title: Max-heap without negation overflow
paragraphs: Construct PriorityQueue<int,int> with Comparer<int>.Create((a,b)=>b.CompareTo(a)). Reversing comparison changes priority order without arithmetic. Do not write b-a: subtraction can overflow and violate comparison ordering. Negating priorities also fails at int.MinValue unless you widen first.

MaxHeapRoot handles int.MinValue and int.MaxValue without special cases. The queue compares priorities, not payloads, so changing only the payload does not affect ordering. Use the same comparer interpretation in every enqueue and dequeue.

sections.title: FIFO queue
paragraphs: Enqueue appends; Dequeue removes the oldest element; Peek reads it; Count reports queued elements. TryDequeue avoids an empty-queue exception when absence is expected. Enqueue is amortized O(1), and normal dequeue is O(1). Use Queue<T> for BFS so earlier discoveries leave before later discoveries.

During level BFS, capture Count before the inner loop. Count changes as items are removed and children added. Ordinary Queue<T> is not a concurrent work queue; thread safety requires a different design or synchronization.

sections.title: LIFO stack
paragraphs: Push adds at the top, Pop removes the most recent item, and Peek reads it. TryPop handles expected emptiness. Push is amortized O(1); Pop and Peek are O(1). Use a stack for explicit DFS or nested obligations such as brackets.

A stack does not magically reverse arbitrary shared mutable data: it reverses the order in which stored items are removed. If stored items are references, mutating the referenced objects still affects those same objects.

sections.title: Both ends with LinkedList<T>
paragraphs: In the .NET 8 baseline used here, LinkedList<T> provides deque behavior through AddFirst/AddLast and RemoveFirst/RemoveLast. First and Last are nullable node references; check Count or null before reading Value. These endpoint operations are O(1).

A linked list allocates nodes and has poorer locality than an array-backed ring buffer. It is adequate for interview clarity; a purpose-built deque can be better for performance. Do not confuse removing a known node (O(1)) with finding a node by value (O(n)).

guides.title: C# maps, sets, ordered keys, and iteration
guides.summary: Lookup semantics matter as much as the method names.

sections.title: TryGetValue and missing defaults
paragraphs: TryGetValue performs one lookup and separately tells you whether a key exists. The out value is default when missing, so do not infer presence from the value itself: zero may be a real stored value. ContainsKey followed by the indexer is valid but performs repeated lookup when you also need the value.

GetValueOrDefault is convenient when a missing value should equal a chosen default, such as a frequency of zero. It does not insert. Expected dictionary lookup is O(1), with cost also depending on hashing/equality of the key; hashing a long string is not free.

sections.title: Incrementing a frequency map
paragraphs: Read the previous frequency (zero if absent), then assign previous+1. The complete Frequencies method demonstrates TryGetValue; counts[c]=counts.GetValueOrDefault(c)+1 is the compact equivalent. An indexer assignment inserts a missing key or replaces an existing value.

For a sliding window, decrement on removal and delete zero-count keys if dictionary.Count represents current distinct symbols. For counting arbitrarily large streams, int counts can overflow; a bounded in-memory string has an int length, so its per-character count fits int.

sections.title: HashSet is membership with uniqueness
paragraphs: HashSet<T>.Add returns true only when the value was absent. That makes if(seen.Add(value)) useful for discovery-time work. Contains checks membership and Remove reports whether an element was removed. It stores no multiplicity, so it cannot replace a frequency map in a counting problem.

Equality comparers define uniqueness. For string identifiers, explicitly choose ordinal or another required comparer rather than accidentally implementing a different case policy. Expected Add/Contains/Remove cost O(1), retained memory O(distinct items).

sections.title: SortedSet and SortedDictionary
paragraphs: SortedSet<T> stores unique values in comparer order; SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue> stores keys in comparer order. Typical lookup/insertion/removal costs O(log n). Use them when you need ordered iteration or range-related operations, not merely because a problem mentions sorting once.

The comparer decides when keys are equal for ordering, so it must be consistent and transitive. The sample uses StringComparer.Ordinal for ordered string keys. Min/Max may require walking a tree path and should not be assumed O(1). An unordered dictionary plus a one-time sort may be simpler for a final sorted report.

sections.title: Do not rely on a blanket enumeration rule
paragraphs: Many structural modifications invalidate a collection’s enumerator, but behavior depends on the collection, operation, and runtime version. Modern Dictionary implementations permit some removals/clears without invalidating enumeration; adding elements is still not a generally safe enumeration strategy.

A portable interview pattern is to snapshot the keys (new List<string>(dictionary.Keys)), iterate that stable snapshot, and perform planned removals on the dictionary. This adds O(n) memory and time for the copy. Alternatively collect removals first and apply them after enumeration. Do not mutate the copied list while enumerating it either.

guides.title: C# sorting and built-in binary search
guides.summary: Know what the library mutates and what its return value means.

sections.title: Sorting intervals by a key
paragraphs: Use Array.Sort(intervals,(a,b)=>a[0].CompareTo(b[0])) to order by start. For List<T>, use list.Sort with the same comparator. CompareTo avoids the overflow risk of a[0]-b[0]. If equal-start ordering matters, add an end-value tie-breaker instead of relying on sort stability.

Array.Sort mutates the outer array. The sample clones that outer array first, preserving input order but sharing inner interval rows; changing a row afterward still affects the original. A deep copy is needed if you plan to mutate the interval values. Sorting costs O(n log n) comparisons.

sections.title: Descending order
paragraphs: Array.Sort followed by Array.Reverse gives descending order in place. A reverse comparer is another option. OrderByDescending(...).ToArray() creates a materialized sorted result and requires System.Linq; leaving off ToArray produces a deferred enumerable rather than an array.

Use a copy when preserving input order matters, and account for that allocation. Sorting to find one maximum is unnecessary O(n log n) work when a single O(n) scan suffices. Decide whether the goal is one extremum, top-k, or complete ordering before selecting the tool.

sections.title: Negative return is a complemented insertion point
paragraphs: Array.BinarySearch assumes the array is sorted under a compatible comparer. A nonnegative result is an index containing an equal value. A negative result encodes the insertion point with bitwise complement: apply ~result to recover it. It is not simply -result.

For duplicate values, a successful search may return any matching occurrence; it is not a lower-bound operation. Use a custom boundary search when the first/last occurrence is required. The sample FindOrInsertionPoint deliberately combines “a found index” and “an insertion point” into one result and documents that ambiguity.
sections.example: In [2,6], searching 4 returns ~1 (which is -2); applying ~ again yields insertion index 1.

guides.title: C# text construction and character contracts
guides.summary: A char is one UTF-16 code unit, not every possible human character.

sections.title: Building a string incrementally
paragraphs: Strings are immutable. Repeatedly appending to a growing string in a loop can copy the accumulated prefix each time, leading to quadratic total character copying. StringBuilder keeps a mutable buffer structure; Append adds pieces, and ToString produces the final immutable string.

This is a practical default for many incremental appends, not a ban on every use of +. A small fixed concatenation or interpolation is clearer and can be optimized by the compiler/runtime. If you already have all pieces, string.Join is usually simpler. Pre-sizing the builder can reduce resizing when a reliable length is known.

sections.title: Lowercase indexing requires an alphabet promise
paragraphs: c-'a' maps lowercase ASCII a-z to 0..25 because those code values are contiguous. Reverse with (char)('a'+index). Validate the character or index before indexing a 26-element array. Uppercase letters, accented letters, and arbitrary Unicode text violate that contract.

C# char and string indexing operate on UTF-16 code units. A Unicode scalar can span two chars, and a displayed grapheme may span several scalars. Clarify whether the interview guarantees lowercase English letters, ASCII, Unicode scalars, or user-perceived characters; the required representation changes accordingly.

sections.title: Join versus constructing from characters
paragraphs: string.Join(separator,values) formats a collection with separators. new string(charArray) creates a string from consecutive characters, and s.ToCharArray() creates a mutable copy of a string’s UTF-16 units. These allocate output/copies; they are not zero-cost views.

Reversing char units can split surrogate pairs or reverse combining marks, so ArrayStringApis.ReverseCopy is a code-unit reversal demonstration, not a general international-text reversal. If a question asks to print an integer list, JoinIntegers returns comma-separated values without a trailing delimiter.

sections.title: Jagged is not automatically rectangular
paragraphs: int[][] is an array of row references. Rows can be null or have different lengths. int[,] is a rectangular multidimensional array with two indices. Many coding platforms use jagged signatures, but inspect the supplied signature rather than assuming a universal platform rule.

Before reading grid[0].Length, handle an empty outer array. Before applying one column count to every row, rely on a stated rectangular contract or validate it. The reference grid methods validate shape; AllocateGrid creates one distinct row array for every row.

sections.title: Allocation and initialization
paragraphs: new int[n] is initialized to zeros; new bool[n] to false; a reference array starts with null entries. Array.Fill(array,-1) replaces every entry. For a jagged bool grid, allocate the outer array and then each row separately.

If you reuse the same row object for every slot, changing one apparent row changes them all. For rectangular storage, new int[m,n] allocates one multidimensional object. State both element count and representation when estimating space; an n×n int table uses roughly 4n² bytes for values alone.

sections.title: Tuples in queues, keys, and comparisons
paragraphs: Queue<(int Row,int Column)> can store coordinates without a custom class; deconstruct a removed value with var (r,c)=queue.Dequeue(). Named elements improve readability but are not separate runtime identity. Value tuples are value types and are useful dictionary keys when their component equality matches the state.

The default comparer for comparable tuple components orders lexicographically, so Array.Sort on (int,int) coordinates sorts row first, then column. C# does not provide tuple < or > syntax, and arbitrary component types may not be orderable. Equality support and ordering support are distinct.

sections.title: Create only when absent
paragraphs: The expression child ??= new Node() evaluates the right side only if child is null, then assigns it. It is convenient in trie insertion and lazy initialization. It does not make initialization thread-safe or validate an array index.

For a nullable child reference, once the operation completes normally the child is non-null. The complete Trie.cs implementation validates lowercase input first and shows the operation in a working data structure rather than an isolated placeholder.

guides.title: C# overflow, sentinels, and safe bounds
guides.summary: Choose the numeric type before arithmetic occurs.

sections.title: Widen an operand, not only the destination
paragraphs: Assigning a*b to a long does not fix an overflow that already happened in int arithmetic. Cast an operand first: (long)a*b. Similarly, (long)a+b widens the sum before evaluation. Summing 100,000 values near one billion needs about 10^14, comfortably beyond int.

Use checked when overflow should fail rather than wrap, and state the supported numeric range. long is larger, not infinite. For unbounded counts, BigInteger may be appropriate, with time and memory depending on bit length. The examples use long for sums and products under explicit input bounds.

sections.title: Infinity is a state, not a normal addend
paragraphs: int.MaxValue, int.MinValue, and long.MaxValue are finite extreme values. If long.MaxValue means “unreachable,” test for that state before adding an edge weight. Adding to a sentinel can overflow or produce a plausible but meaningless value.

A sentinel can collide with legitimate data. Nullable values, a Try method, or a separate boolean is often safer for “missing.” double.PositiveInfinity follows floating-point rules and should not be substituted into exact integer arithmetic without considering precision.

sections.title: Midpoint safety depends on the bounds
paragraphs: lo+(hi-lo)/2 avoids overflow from lo+hi when lo and hi are nonnegative int array indices and their difference fits int. Across the full signed int range, hi-lo can itself overflow. Numerics.Midpoint widens both the difference and addition to long before converting the in-range midpoint back to int.

For full-range long bounds, a further strategy is needed: narrower documented bounds, unsigned arithmetic with a proof, or BigInteger. Never label a formula universally overflow-safe without stating its domain. In answer-search examples here, nonnegative capacities fit long and their difference also fits.
sections.example: Midpoint(int.MinValue,int.MaxValue) is -1 with the widened calculation; doing hi-lo in int is unsafe.

guides.title: Memoization and recursion depth
guides.summary: Caching repeated states changes work, but does not remove the call stack.

sections.title: Cache by the complete logical state
paragraphs: Memoization stores the answer to a subproblem so later visits avoid recomputing it. In LCS, the pair (i,j) identifies remaining suffixes, so a Dictionary<(int,int),int> is a valid key. Query it after base cases; compute and store on a miss. Zero is a valid cached answer, so TryGetValue must decide presence.

A key must include every input that can change the answer. If a backtracking result depends on a visited set or remaining budget, caching only the current coordinate is wrong. Likewise, keep the memo local or clear it when the original input changes. Number of states times work per state is the useful complexity model: LCS has O(mn) states.

sections.title: Recursion can still be linear depth
paragraphs: A skewed tree, a long linked list, or a thin grid component can make recursion depth O(n). The safe depth depends on runtime stack size and frame size, so there is no universal safe cutoff such as 100,000. C# does not guarantee tail-call optimization for ordinary recursive methods.

Convert to an explicit stack or iterative DP when depth can be large. Preserve the work that recursion was doing: a postorder computation may need frames with an “expanded” flag or saved child results, while a simple reachability DFS needs only node identities. Memoization reduces repeated branches but may leave the longest chain unchanged.

guides.title: Read constraints as a budget, not a lookup table
guides.summary: Estimate actual work and memory, then choose the simplest feasible algorithm.

sections.title: n around 10–12: factorial output is already large
paragraphs: n! counts permutations, but “n<=12” does not guarantee a factorial algorithm is fast enough. 10! is 3,628,800; 12! is 479,001,600. Materializing every 12-element permutation requires billions of stored integers before object overhead. Even generating without storing has enormous output cost.

Use small-n constraints as permission to investigate exhaustive search, pruning, symmetry reduction, or dynamic programming over subsets. Estimate nodes visited and cost per leaf, not only the asymptotic label. If the prompt literally requires all permutations, explain that output size itself limits scaling.

sections.title: n around 20–25: subsets may be borderline
paragraphs: 2^20 is about one million and 2^25 about 33.6 million. A constant-time bit operation per subset differs radically from copying 25 items or scanning all pairs for every subset. O(n·2^n) and O(2^n) are not interchangeable budgets.

Bitmask DP can fit some small-n optimization tasks, but it is an advanced follow-on here. First learn ordinary backtracking and one-dimensional DP. Count states, transitions, memory per state, and output volume before deciding enumeration is acceptable.

sections.title: n around 100: cubic can be plausible; quartic is costly
paragraphs: 100^3 is one million inner operations, while 100^4 is one hundred million. These are different practical workloads even before allocation, hashing, or complex transitions. A “2-D DP” label does not imply O(n³) or O(n⁴): dimensions and transition work determine time.

Floyd-Warshall is O(V³) for all-pairs paths, interval DP is often O(n³), and simple two-string DP is O(mn). Identify the actual loops. Do not memorize a range as a promise that every algorithm within it meets an unspecified time limit.

sections.title: n around 500: verify cubic cost carefully
paragraphs: 500³ is 125 million iterations. That may be too slow for a heavy C# transition or tight interview platform budget. A 500×500 int table has roughly one million bytes of element payload, but additional object structures can cost much more.

Compare the known O(n³) approach to possible O(n²) or O(n² log n) alternatives, but avoid inventing an optimization you cannot justify. State estimated work and ask about time/memory limits if they are absent.

sections.title: n around 5,000: quadratic is 25 million
paragraphs: A simple O(n²) loop at 5,000 elements does around 25 million iterations (or half that for unordered pairs). A 5,000² int table is about 100 MB of payload, which may exceed memory limits even when the running time is acceptable.

A streaming pair comparison and a full pair table have the same time order but different memory requirements. Rolling rows, two-pointer elimination, or hashing may help when their invariants match the problem. Treat both time and space as first-class constraints.

sections.title: n around 100,000: sorting is a useful baseline
paragraphs: n log2 n is about 1.7 million at n=100,000, while n² is ten billion. This often rules out all pairs and makes sorting, heaps, or balanced trees attractive. The exact constant factors and the cost of comparison still matter.

Hash-based O(n) expected-time algorithms can beat sorting, but sorting may be deterministic, compact, and simpler. Choose the cleanest approach satisfying the budget, and distinguish expected, amortized, and worst-case complexity.

sections.title: Millions of elements: scans and memory traffic matter
paragraphs: At n=10^6 to 10^7, a few linear passes may be appropriate, while per-element allocation, large maps, and input parsing can dominate. An int array of ten million elements alone contains about 40 MB of payload. O(n) memory may still be too much.

Sliding windows, prefix sums, and hashing are possible linear techniques, but each has a contract and memory tradeoff. A linear algorithm can perform many expensive operations per item; Big-O does not measure wall-clock time directly.

sections.title: A huge numeric range is not necessarily huge input
paragraphs: A numeric bound such as 10^18 may describe an answer range, not a count of stored elements. Binary searching that integer range needs roughly 60 predicate checks, but each check might scan an input of size n, for total O(n log range).

If n really is the length of an explicitly supplied unsorted array, reading it alone costs Ω(n); you cannot usually solve an arbitrary property in O(log n). Large value ranges suggest arithmetic or answer search only when the problem structure supports them.

guides.title: A repeatable coding interview workflow
guides.summary: Make your reasoning inspectable and your assumptions testable.

sections.title: Think aloud at useful decision points
paragraphs: Explain the goal, the current hypothesis, and why you are testing it. If stuck, say what is failing: “The nested loop is correct but quadratic; I’m looking for a way to reuse work between adjacent windows.” That gives the interviewer something concrete to respond to.

There is no universal 20-second silence rule, and interviewers differ in how they give hints. Short quiet thinking is normal. Avoid narrating every keystroke; instead signal assumptions, invariants, changes of approach, and test results. If you need a moment, say so briefly.

sections.title: Clarify, baseline, improve, implement, test
paragraphs: Restate the input/output contract: duplicates, empty input, index base, mutation permission, ordering, and numeric bounds. Give a correct baseline before optimizing. Explain the key invariant and target time/space, then check for questions if the interviewer is engaging. You do not need a ritual permission request before every implementation.

After coding, trace a small normal example and purposeful edge cases: empty/singleton, duplicates, missing target, extreme values, disconnected graph, or invalid shape as relevant. Explain any validation you omit because constraints guarantee it. Keep an unaided first attempt before opening this guide; afterward record the actual gap (recognition, derivation, C# syntax, correctness, or speed), not just whether the final code looks familiar.

Interview formats vary by company and round, including whether AI tools are permitted. Verify the current instructions for the specific role rather than assuming a universal environment. This curriculum supports reasoning and implementation you can perform independently; it is not a guarantee of every possible interview topic.
sections.example: A concise plan: “I’ll keep prior values in a map so each number needs one complement lookup. That is expected O(n) time and O(n) memory. I’ll test duplicate values and no match.”

guides.title: Graph modeling before traversal
guides.summary: Define vertices, edges, direction, and visited state before choosing BFS or DFS.

sections.title: Adjacency lists and disconnected components
paragraphs: An adjacency list stores each vertex’s outgoing neighbors. For an undirected edge add both directions; for a directed edge add only the stated direction. Explicitly create all vertices, including isolated ones. For a graph with V vertices and E edges, lists typically use O(V+E) storage, while an adjacency matrix uses O(V²).

A traversal from one start reaches only its component. To cover the whole graph, loop over every vertex and start a new traversal for each unseen one. Mark on scheduling so cycles cannot keep adding work. Graphs.Components supplies an iterative undirected example, including isolated nodes and an empty graph.

The state may be richer than the visible node: a puzzle can use board configurations as vertices, while a constrained route can use (location,remainingBudget). A visited set keyed too coarsely can incorrectly prune a solution. Conversely, a tree normally needs no visited set if the input is truly acyclic and child pointers never lead upward.

Before coding, state whether self-loops or repeated edges are allowed, whether the graph is directed, and whether you need reachability, a shortest path, a dependency order, or connectivity under updates. These are different outputs even when the same adjacency list can represent them.

guides.title: Asynchronous replication: two different promises
guides.summary: The write avoids waiting for that replica, but replica reads can lag. Promoting an out-of-date replica after primary failure can lose acknowledged writes. Define acceptable staleness and data loss separately; replication alone does not imply read-after-write consistency.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: The write avoids waiting for that replica, but replica reads can lag. Promoting an out-of-date replica after primary failure can lose acknowledged writes. Define acceptable staleness and data loss separately; replication alone does not imply read-after-write consistency.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Follow the write through four moments: primary commits, client receives success, replica receives the log, replica replays it. Acknowledging at the second moment leaves the last two unfinished. Distinguish data durability after failover from freshness of reads during healthy operation.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: At 10:00:00 an account name becomes Ada on the primary. The reply arrives at 10:00:00.020, but replica replay finishes at 10:00:00.300. A read at 10:00:00.100 can return the old name. If the primary is irrecoverably lost before transfer, promoting that replica can also lose the change. These are two different failure stories.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Route freshness-sensitive reads to the authoritative node, or wait for a specific replication position.
Measure replica lag and test failover loss; average healthy-state lag is not a maximum-loss guarantee.
Choose asynchronous replication when lower write latency and replica unavailability tolerance justify the stated loss window.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Explain why “three copies” says little without the acknowledgement policy. What happens if the primary dies immediately after success?

guides.title: Synchronous replication: define the acknowledgement
guides.summary: Specify which replicas acknowledge and whether acknowledgement means receipt, durable storage, or application. Waiting adds latency and can block commits when required replicas are unavailable. Durable acknowledgement does not mean every replica can already serve the new value.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Specify which replicas acknowledge and whether acknowledgement means receipt, durable storage, or application. Waiting adds latency and can block commits when required replicas are unavailable. Durable acknowledgement does not mean every replica can already serve the new value.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A synchronous commit waits for a configured set of replicas to reach a specified point. Receipt in memory, durable log flush, and replay for queries are different points. Requiring more remote acknowledgements can strengthen a failure guarantee while increasing latency and the number of failures that block progress.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Imagine A is the primary and B and C are replicas. A waits for B to flush its log, then replies. B can recover the log after a crash, but a query on B may wait for replay. C was not required at all. “A synchronous write” therefore does not justify sending an immediate read to arbitrary C.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Name which node failures you intend to survive. Separate local durability, remote durability, and read visibility.
A slow required replica can increase tail latency. Decide whether to block or deliberately weaken the policy during failures.
Synchronous replicas still do not replace backups against application deletion or corruption.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Draw the acknowledgement boundary. Which exact replica can safely serve the next read, and under what replay condition?

guides.title: Partition keys: distribution versus hot traffic
guides.summary: Hashing spreads distinct keys, not the requests for one key. A heavily accessed key can dominate one partition even when key counts are balanced. Evaluate traffic and item sizes per key, plus secondary-index access patterns, rather than relying on aggregate table capacity.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Hashing spreads distinct keys, not the requests for one key. A heavily accessed key can dominate one partition even when key counts are balanced. Evaluate traffic and item sizes per key, plus secondary-index access patterns, rather than relying on aggregate table capacity.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A partition function chooses where a key lives. It does not divide the work for a single key. Compare per-key request frequency, bytes, and write contention; uniform counts of stored keys can coexist with extremely uneven traffic.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: One million customers are evenly hashed across 100 partitions. One customer sends 40% of all writes. Its partition receives those writes plus roughly its normal share of the remaining traffic. Adding cold customers changes key-count balance but does nothing to that hot customer.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Cache repeated reads where freshness permits; write hotspots usually need a different key or data model.
Bucket time-series writes or add shards only if readers can locate or merge the pieces.
A secondary index can introduce its own hot key even when the base-table key is balanced.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Ask whether the hot unit is an entire tenant, one record, or a global counter. Why can only some of these be split without changing semantics?

guides.title: Indexes: pay on writes to save selected reads
guides.summary: Indexes accelerate suitable lookups but require storage and maintenance when data changes. Choose them from important access patterns and verify the query plan. A planner may prefer a sequential scan when the index would not save enough work; an unused index still imposes costs.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Indexes accelerate suitable lookups but require storage and maintenance when data changes. Choose them from important access patterns and verify the query plan. A planner may prefer a sequential scan when the index would not save enough work; an unused index still imposes costs.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A B-tree maintains sorted searchable entries pointing toward rows. A useful index narrows the candidate range before fetching data. Every indexed insert, delete, and relevant update may also maintain this extra structure, and the structure consumes cache and storage.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: An orders table is commonly queried by tenant and recent creation time. An index aligned with that access path can avoid scanning other tenants. An index on an unfiltered notes field does not help that query, yet all incoming orders still pay its maintenance cost.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Start with a high-value query, its predicates, ordering, output columns, and measured plan.
Low-selectivity queries can legitimately scan. An index seek followed by many random row lookups may be worse.
Write throughput, storage, vacuum or maintenance, and memory pressure belong in the decision.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Given three candidate indexes, explain which measured access pattern each serves and what redundant work it adds.

guides.title: Transactions do not automatically protect every invariant
guides.summary: No. PostgreSQL’s default Read Committed isolation gives each statement a snapshot, so concurrent transactions can still violate a multi-statement business invariant. Use suitable constraints, locking, or Serializable isolation for the invariant. Serializable transactions can abort on conflicts; retry the entire transaction, including its reads.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. PostgreSQL’s default Read Committed isolation gives each statement a snapshot, so concurrent transactions can still violate a multi-statement business invariant. Use suitable constraints, locking, or Serializable isolation for the invariant. Serializable transactions can abort on conflicts; retry the entire transaction, including its reads.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Atomicity says a transaction commits all its database changes or none. Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe and how conflicts are handled. Read Committed does not turn a multi-statement decision into a serial execution of the entire business operation.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy roster requires at least one doctor on call. Two transactions each read that two doctors are present. Each removes a different doctor and commits. Individual row updates can succeed while the cross-row invariant fails. A transaction around each sequence was not sufficient.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Prefer an enforceable constraint when the invariant can be expressed by the database.
Otherwise serialize the relevant decision with appropriate locks or use Serializable with whole-transaction retry.
Keep network calls outside held database locks when possible; they extend contention and do not join database atomicity.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Name the invariant before naming an isolation level. Explain which concurrent interleaving your solution prevents.

guides.title: Cache-aside and its stale-fill race
guides.summary: No. A miss loads the database value into the cache, but invalidation races or writes outside the cache path can leave stale entries. Update the database before invalidating its cached value, while recognizing that this order alone does not eliminate every race. Choose TTLs and stronger coordination according to the freshness requirement.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. A miss loads the database value into the cache, but invalidation races or writes outside the cache path can leave stale entries. Update the database before invalidating its cached value, while recognizing that this order alone does not eliminate every race. Choose TTLs and stronger coordination according to the freshness requirement.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: The application checks a cache; on a miss it reads the source and stores the result. Writes change the source and typically invalidate the cached copy. A TTL bounds residence after a fill, but does not itself coordinate readers and writers.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Reader R misses and reads version 1. Writer W commits version 2 and deletes the cache entry. R now stores version 1. The recommended database-then-invalidate order did not prevent this in-flight stale fill. A five-minute TTL may leave version 1 visible for five more minutes.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Use cache-aside for read-heavy data with an explicit freshness allowance.
Versioned keys or version-aware writes can avoid overwriting newer state; coordination adds complexity.
For strict reads, bypass this cache or use a design with a stronger verified consistency contract.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Walk through the race using R and W. What does your freshness requirement permit, and what does your TTL actually bound?

guides.title: Idempotency keys represent an intention
guides.summary: Two intentional operations can have identical parameters. A stable operation ID distinguishes one operation’s retries from a new operation. Scope the ID to the caller and operation, reject conflicting reuse, and retain the outcome for the supported retry window. Recording the ID and applying the effect must be atomic or recoverable.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Two intentional operations can have identical parameters. A stable operation ID distinguishes one operation’s retries from a new operation. Scope the ID to the caller and operation, reject conflicting reuse, and retain the outcome for the supported retry window. Recording the ID and applying the effect must be atomic or recoverable.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: An operation key identifies one logical request across transport retries. Store its request fingerprint, status, and outcome. The key namespace must include the relevant caller or tenant. Same key plus conflicting input should fail rather than silently reuse a different result.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A shopper intentionally buys the same book twice on different days. Both bodies are identical, but the operation keys are K1 and K2. A network retry of the first purchase reuses K1. Deduplicating by body hash would incorrectly merge the two intentional purchases.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Use a unique database constraint so two concurrent requests cannot both claim the key.
Make the effect and durable idempotency record atomic, or persist a resumable state machine that can reconcile uncertainty.
Define retention, in-progress responses, and whether failures are retained. A retry after expiry may be a new operation.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Explain the crash between performing an effect and saving its result. How is a later retry resolved?

guides.title: Retries need a deadline and a spread
guides.summary: Backoff spaces out one client’s retries; jitter spreads retries from many clients so they do not return together. Also cap attempts or elapsed time and retry only appropriate failures. Backoff with jitter reduces synchronization, but unlimited retries can still overload a dependency.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Backoff spaces out one client’s retries; jitter spreads retries from many clients so they do not return together. Also cap attempts or elapsed time and retry only appropriate failures. Backoff with jitter reduces synchronization, but unlimited retries can still overload a dependency.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Exponential backoff increases the delay between attempts. Jitter varies delays between callers, breaking synchronized bursts. Neither makes a permanently invalid request useful, and retries consume real capacity from a dependency that may already be failing.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: For attempt n, one illustrative full-jitter delay is uniform(0, min(2 seconds, 100 milliseconds × 2^n)). Ten thousand callers do not all wake at precisely 100, 200, and 400 milliseconds. Still stop at the overall deadline and use the same operation key for a retried create.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Separate connection, per-attempt, and overall operation deadlines. Account for work already attempted.
Retry only classified transient failures and safe or idempotent operations; honor service guidance such as Retry-After.
A bounded retry budget and concurrency limit protect a recovering dependency.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: What happens if the first attempt succeeds but its reply is lost? Backoff is not the answer to that correctness question.

guides.title: A queue buys time, not processing capacity
guides.summary: No. A queue buffers bursts and separates intake from processing, but backlog grows if average arrival rate exceeds completion rate. Monitor backlog age and depth. Increase safe processing capacity, limit intake, or shed work; unrestricted worker scaling can simply overload the downstream database.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. A queue buffers bursts and separates intake from processing, but backlog grows if average arrival rate exceeds completion rate. Monitor backlog age and depth. Increase safe processing capacity, limit intake, or shed work; unrestricted worker scaling can simply overload the downstream database.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Backlog changes by arrivals minus completions. A queue absorbs a temporary mismatch and lets workers run independently of request intake. When the long-term arrival rate exceeds sustainable completion rate, backlog and waiting time keep increasing.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy worker fleet completes 80 jobs per second while intake stays at 100. After ten minutes the queue has added about 12,000 jobs. Adding workers helps only if the next bottleneck, such as the database, can sustain the larger load.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Monitor oldest-message age as well as depth; the user cares how long their work is waiting.
Bound intake, worker concurrency, and storage. Choose rejection, deferred admission, or lower-priority shedding deliberately.
Handle poison messages with bounded retries and inspection rather than endlessly blocking useful work.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: After a ten-minute spike ends, how much spare completion capacity exists to drain its backlog, and how long will recovery take?

guides.title: Consumer acknowledgement creates a crash window
guides.summary: Acknowledging first risks losing the work if the consumer crashes before completing it. Acknowledging afterward permits redelivery if the work commits but the acknowledgement is lost. The latter supports at-least-once processing when delivery is retried, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Acknowledging first risks losing the work if the consumer crashes before completing it. Acknowledging afterward permits redelivery if the work commits but the acknowledgement is lost. The latter supports at-least-once processing when delivery is retried, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: The broker needs evidence that it can stop tracking a delivery. Acknowledging before the business effect risks lost work. Committing first and acknowledging second creates a duplicate window. At-least-once delivery therefore needs a duplicate-safe effect.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A worker receives message M, adds a loyalty credit, commits, and crashes before ack. The broker later redelivers M. A transactional unique processed-message record lets the next worker recognize that the credit was already committed.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Publisher confirmation is a separate leg; it does not prove consumer work completed.
Acknowledge only after durable success under the intended business contract.
Bound unacknowledged deliveries so a slow consumer does not accumulate unlimited work in memory.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Draw the crash immediately before and immediately after each step. Which failures cause loss and which cause duplicates?

guides.title: Tail latency: measure the slow experience
guides.summary: A fast majority can hide a slow tail. Inspect a latency distribution and relevant percentiles, and distinguish successful from failed requests. A page that depends on several services can expose users to slow outliers frequently. Define the measurement window and measure the end-to-end user operation as well as dependencies.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: A fast majority can hide a slow tail. Inspect a latency distribution and relevant percentiles, and distinguish successful from failed requests. A page that depends on several services can expose users to slow outliers frequently. Define the measurement window and measure the end-to-end user operation as well as dependencies.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A percentile describes a point in a measured latency distribution. The mean can stay small while a meaningful fraction of users wait seconds. Fan-out makes slow dependencies especially important because the user operation often waits for its slowest required branch.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Of 100 toy requests, 99 finish in 10 ms and one in 5,000 ms. The mean is 59.9 ms, but the unlucky user waited five seconds. If many independent branches each have a slow tail, an operation needing all branches encounters an outlier more frequently.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Measure end-to-end latency, including queueing, and name the window and eligible requests.
Separate successes and failures; fast failures can make a latency metric look deceptively healthy.
Percentiles cannot generally be averaged across hosts. Merge suitable distributions or histograms.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: If p50 is stable and p99 doubles, investigate saturation, lock contention, pauses, slow I/O, and request mix before adding arbitrary replicas.

guides.title: Capacity belongs to a workload and an SLO
guides.summary: Request costs differ. Tie the rate to a workload mix, payload sizes, and latency target, then measure the limiting resources such as CPU, memory, network, or storage I/O. A change in query mix can invalidate a request-rate estimate even if total traffic is unchanged.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Request costs differ. Tie the rate to a workload mix, payload sizes, and latency target, then measure the limiting resources such as CPU, memory, network, or storage I/O. A change in query mix can invalidate a request-rate estimate even if total traffic is unchanged.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A request is not a unit of equal cost. Throughput depends on query work, payloads, CPU time, I/O, concurrency, and required latency. As utilization approaches a limiting resource, queueing can increase latency long before outright errors appear.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A read endpoint serves cached 1 KB objects cheaply. A report endpoint scans millions of rows and serializes 10 MB. “1,000 requests per second” predicts little until the mix is known. A load test that warms every cache can miss a cold-start collapse.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Estimate bytes, CPU or I/O per operation, peak concurrency, and fan-out; then validate with a realistic load test.
Include headroom for node loss, bursts, background maintenance, and uneven tenants.
Report capacity at a latency and error target, rather than at the point where the server barely avoids crashing.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Which resource saturates first, and what signal would prove that diagnosis rather than simply correlate with it?

guides.title: SLOs turn reliability into a measurable decision
guides.summary: Define what counts as a good event and the measurement window. The allowed fraction of bad events is the error budget: a 99.9% request-success target allows 0.1% failures among eligible requests. Agree on actions when the budget is consumed, such as prioritizing reliability work or limiting risky releases.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Define what counts as a good event and the measurement window. The allowed fraction of bad events is the error budget: a 99.9% request-success target allows 0.1% failures among eligible requests. Agree on actions when the budget is consumed, such as prioritizing reliability work or limiting risky releases.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: An SLI is the observed indicator, an SLO is its target, and an error budget is the permitted bad portion over the chosen window. Select eligible events and the definition of good carefully so the metric represents user experience.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: For a toy month with 2,000,000 eligible operations and a 99.9% success SLO, the budget is 2,000 bad operations. If 1,500 fail in the first week, 500 remain under that simple event-based accounting. This is not automatically equivalent to a fixed number of downtime minutes.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Define latency and correctness goals where “HTTP 200” alone misses a bad experience.
Choose alerting and release policies before an incident; use consumption rate to distinguish urgent loss from small noise.
Do not promise 100% without confronting the cost and the meaning of dependencies.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: What decision changes when the budget is being exhausted? A target with no operational consequence is only a dashboard number.

guides.title: RPO and RTO: loss and downtime are different
guides.summary: RPO limits acceptable data loss, expressed as a time window. RTO limits acceptable time to restore service. A low RPO drives backup or replication frequency; a low RTO drives recovery readiness and automation. Set them from business impact and dependencies, then validate the design with recovery tests.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: RPO limits acceptable data loss, expressed as a time window. RTO limits acceptable time to restore service. A low RPO drives backup or replication frequency; a low RTO drives recovery readiness and automation. Set them from business impact and dependencies, then validate the design with recovery tests.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: RPO describes how old the recovered state may be relative to failure; RTO describes the acceptable recovery duration. A frequent backup can improve the first while leaving a slow manual restore for the second.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy service permits 15 minutes of data loss and one hour of downtime. Hourly backups alone miss the RPO. Five-minute backups might meet that loss goal, but a three-hour restore misses the RTO. Measure the complete path from detecting failure to restored useful service.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Include database, identity, secrets, DNS, object storage, and external dependencies in recovery exercises.
Replicas can faithfully copy corruption or accidental deletion; retain recoverable historical state.
Choose objectives from user impact and cost, then test actual restoration instead of inferring it from a backup-success email.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: If a restore drill exceeds RTO, which step dominates: provisioning, data transfer, replay, validation, or traffic cutover?

sources.title: AWS Reliability Pillar: Define recovery objectives for downtime and data loss

guides.title: One database transaction, one atomic boundary
guides.summary: It makes the database changes commit together or roll back together, preventing an observer from seeing a partly committed operation. This is useful when the related state fits one database transaction. An HTTP call or message publication outside that transaction does not become atomic merely because the database work is transactional.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: It makes the database changes commit together or roll back together, preventing an observer from seeing a partly committed operation. This is useful when the related state fits one database transaction. An HTTP call or message publication outside that transaction does not become atomic merely because the database work is transactional.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A transaction groups related changes so committed state does not contain only half the operation. Constraints and suitable isolation are still required for correctness under concurrency. Database rollback cannot unsend an external HTTP request.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: In a toy order database, insert the order and its order lines in one transaction. If a line violates a constraint, roll back the order too. If sending a confirmation email fails after commit, the database cannot roll back the email system; record pending notification work durably.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Keep transactions short and avoid user interaction while locks are held.
Handle the commit-result-unknown case after a connection failure using a stable business operation ID.
Use an outbox to connect committed state to eventual message publication.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: List every effect in the operation and mark which can actually join this transaction. Treat the remaining effects explicitly.

guides.title: Composite indexes follow the access path
guides.summary: A composite index on (tenant_id, created_at): the leading equality narrows the tenant, then the range narrows its records. Verify with the actual query plan and data distribution. Queries filtering only created_at may need a different index; do not assume either that this index is ideal or that it is never usable.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: A composite index on (tenant_id, created_at): the leading equality narrows the tenant, then the range narrows its records. Verify with the actual query plan and data distribution. Queries filtering only created_at may need a different index; do not assume either that this index is ideal or that it is never usable.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A composite B-tree orders by the first key, then the next within equal preceding keys. Equality on tenant followed by a time range naturally fits (tenant_id, created_at). Additional output columns may change whether row lookups are needed.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: For tenant 7 and dates from October 1 through October 2, the index can locate that tenant’s slice and walk the relevant dates. A query for all tenants on October 1 is a different access path. Test its plan rather than asserting the existing index can never help.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Use realistic cardinality and skew when checking estimated and actual plans.
Add a unique tiebreaker when ordering and pagination need a stable sequence.
An index has write and space costs even when a particular planner chooses a scan.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Write the exact WHERE and ORDER BY before proposing an index. What changes if the equality column becomes a range?

guides.title: Redis cache policy under memory pressure
guides.summary: Set a memory limit and an eviction policy that fits the access pattern, then monitor hits, misses, and evictions. LRU or LFU policies can evict reusable entries; noeviction instead rejects writes that need more memory. TTL expiration and memory-pressure eviction are separate mechanisms. Leave room for process overhead and replication or persistence buffers.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Set a memory limit and an eviction policy that fits the access pattern, then monitor hits, misses, and evictions. LRU or LFU policies can evict reusable entries; noeviction instead rejects writes that need more memory. TTL expiration and memory-pressure eviction are separate mechanisms. Leave room for process overhead and replication or persistence buffers.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: TTL expiration removes keys because time has passed. Eviction removes eligible keys because the memory policy needs room. LRU approximates recent use; LFU approximates frequent use. A noeviction policy can reject memory-growing writes instead of discarding cache entries.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy cache holds catalog pages with one-hour TTLs. A sudden import exceeds its memory budget after five minutes. Entries may be evicted before their TTLs expire. If the application assumes TTL guarantees residency, its miss traffic can unexpectedly hit the database.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Monitor used memory, process overhead, hit rate, misses, evictions, and rejected writes.
Leave room for replication and persistence buffers rather than assigning all machine RAM to data.
Cache contents must be safe to recompute or lose under the chosen policy.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Explain how you would load-test a cold cache and prevent an eviction spiral from saturating the source database.

guides.title: Redis success is not one universal durability guarantee
guides.summary: It depends on persistence and failure mode. With persistence disabled, memory loss loses the dataset. RDB snapshots can lose changes since the last snapshot; AOF durability depends on its fsync policy. Choose and test a loss window appropriate to the data rather than treating a cache acknowledgement as durable database commit.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: It depends on persistence and failure mode. With persistence disabled, memory loss loses the dataset. RDB snapshots can lose changes since the last snapshot; AOF durability depends on its fsync policy. Choose and test a loss window appropriate to the data rather than treating a cache acknowledgement as durable database commit.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Redis can serve memory-resident state with different persistence configurations. Snapshots represent discrete points in time; append-only logging has a synchronization policy. Durability also depends on the failure you are considering, such as process exit versus host or disk loss.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: In a toy deployment, a snapshot at 12:00 is the only persisted copy and the machine fails at 12:08. Writes acknowledged during those eight minutes may disappear on restore. Reconstructible cache entries tolerate this; an authoritative ledger probably does not.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: State the maximum acceptable loss window and validate the selected persistence and replication behavior.
Test restore, not just backup creation. Monitor persistence failures and resource pressure.
Do not treat replication, disk persistence, and historical backups as interchangeable protections.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Which data in Redis is authoritative, and what exactly reconstructs it if every memory copy disappears?

guides.title: Kafka ordering is a partition-level tool
guides.summary: Use customer ID so that customer’s records share a partition under a stable partitioning scheme. Ordering is partition-scoped, and application processing must preserve the order it needs. A busy customer can create a hot partition. Changing partition count or spreading one customer across partitions requires an explicit ordering strategy.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Use customer ID so that customer’s records share a partition under a stable partitioning scheme. Ordering is partition-scoped, and application processing must preserve the order it needs. A busy customer can create a hot partition. Changing partition count or spreading one customer across partitions requires an explicit ordering strategy.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Records in a partition have an ordered log position. Keying by customer can place that customer’s events together under a stable partitioner. Consumer application code must still avoid reordering the business effects, such as launching all deliveries concurrently.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Customer 42 creates event A then event B. Both reach partition 3 in that order. If a worker starts two asynchronous handlers and B finishes first, downstream effects can still occur out of order. The log’s order did not serialize the handlers.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: A hot customer can dominate a single partition, limiting per-customer parallelism.
Changing partition count can change key routing, so plan migration when cross-change order matters.
Define whether the requirement is per customer, per order, or global; global ordering imposes a much tighter bottleneck.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Where is order created, persisted, and preserved during retries? Does the destination accept sequence numbers or reject stale updates?

guides.title: Kafka groups: partitions bound traditional ownership
guides.summary: No, assuming they subscribe only to that topic: at most six can hold assignments because one partition has one consumer owner within a traditional group at a time. More consumers can provide standby capacity. Adding partitions changes the scaling and key-placement tradeoffs; this rule does not describe Kafka share groups.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No, assuming they subscribe only to that topic: at most six can hold assignments because one partition has one consumer owner within a traditional group at a time. More consumers can provide standby capacity. Adding partitions changes the scaling and key-placement tradeoffs; this rule does not describe Kafka share groups.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: In a traditional consumer group, each partition is assigned to one member at a time. A member may own several partitions. More members than subscribed partitions cannot all get assignments, although spare members can help replace failures.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A topic has six partitions and twelve group members subscribe only to it. At most six members receive partition ownership. If one partition carries 80% of traffic, six active members still do not imply balanced work.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Partition count affects parallelism, ordering, rebalancing, and operational overhead.
Track lag per partition and processing time rather than only total topic throughput.
Internal handler concurrency needs careful offset coordination and ordering. Kafka share groups have a different model.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Why might doubling consumers fail to reduce lag? Separate insufficient ownership slots from skew, downstream saturation, and slow handlers.

guides.title: Exactly-once: always state the boundary
guides.summary: No. Kafka transactions can atomically commit output records and consumed offsets for a Kafka-to-Kafka flow, with consumers using read_committed to hide aborted writes. External effects require cooperation from the destination, such as idempotency or atomic storage of the effect with its processing position. State the guarantee’s boundary.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. Kafka transactions can atomically commit output records and consumed offsets for a Kafka-to-Kafka flow, with consumers using read_committed to hide aborted writes. External effects require cooperation from the destination, such as idempotency or atomic storage of the effect with its processing position. State the guarantee’s boundary.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Kafka transactions can coordinate consumed offsets with produced Kafka records. Readers configured to ignore aborted transactions see the committed result of that flow. An arbitrary external side effect does not join Kafka’s transaction just because it is executed inside the handler.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A handler consumes “send email,” sends it through a third-party API, then crashes before recording completion. Reprocessing can send twice. A Kafka transaction cannot undo the first email. A destination-supported idempotency key or durable reconciliation contract is needed.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Describe Kafka-to-Kafka guarantees separately from database, payment, email, or filesystem effects.
Idempotent producers address a producer retry issue; they do not remove every possible business duplicate.
For external storage, coordinate the processing marker and effect within that destination’s atomic boundary when possible.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Ask “exactly once where?” Show the crash after the external effect but before the commit.

guides.title: RabbitMQ confirms and acknowledgements cover different legs
guides.summary: No. A publisher confirm covers the publisher-to-broker leg. A consumer acknowledgement covers the broker-to-consumer leg; these are independent. If the producer needs the business result, add an application-level response or status mechanism. Select queue durability and replication separately from acknowledgement handling.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. A publisher confirm covers the publisher-to-broker leg. A consumer acknowledgement covers the broker-to-consumer leg; these are independent. If the producer needs the business result, add an application-level response or status mechanism. Select queue durability and replication separately from acknowledgement handling.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A publisher confirm reports the broker’s handling of a published message under the queue’s contract. A consumer acknowledgement reports delivery handling back to the broker. The two mechanisms are independent; neither is automatically an application-level business response.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy order producer receives a broker confirm at 09:00. The queue’s worker is paused until 09:05. No shipment has happened at 09:00. If the UI needs completion status, persist a job ID and expose state or send a separate result event.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Choose durable queues, message persistence, replication, and routing failure handling explicitly.
An uncertain publish result may require retransmission, which can create duplicates.
When acknowledgements are delayed, manage prefetch and worker capacity to bound in-flight work.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Which status should the UI display after broker acceptance: accepted, processing, or completed? Explain the evidence for each transition.

guides.title: Object consistency does not create multi-object transactions
guides.summary: Absent a later write, subsequent GET and LIST requests reflect the completed write. Updating one object key is atomic: readers see an old or new object, never a partial object. This does not provide atomic transactions across multiple keys. Cached responses outside S3 have their own freshness rules.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Absent a later write, subsequent GET and LIST requests reflect the completed write. Updating one object key is atomic: readers see an old or new object, never a partial object. This does not provide atomic transactions across multiple keys. Cached responses outside S3 have their own freshness rules.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: S3’s object operations provide strong read-after-write behavior for completed writes. A single key’s object replacement is atomic to readers. A set of related keys does not become one transactional commit, and a separate CDN may still hold an earlier response.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A publisher updates manifest.json and image.jpg as separate requests. A client can observe the new manifest before the image upload completes. A safer publication pattern uploads a new immutable image key first, then updates the manifest that points to it.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Use unique immutable object keys for versioned assets when practical.
Separate origin consistency from CDN or application-cache freshness.
Concurrent writers still need a conflict policy or conditional operations; strong consistency does not decide who should win.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: If a dataset contains 1,000 objects, what indicates it is complete and safe for consumers to discover?

guides.title: Direct uploads with narrowly scoped capabilities
guides.summary: Authorize the upload in the application and issue a short-lived presigned URL for the intended object and method. The client sends bytes directly to S3. Treat the URL as a bearer capability: protect it, limit its scope and lifetime, and choose keys carefully because an upload can replace an existing object at that key.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Authorize the upload in the application and issue a short-lived presigned URL for the intended object and method. The client sends bytes directly to S3. Treat the URL as a bearer capability: protect it, limit its scope and lifetime, and choose keys carefully because an upload can replace an existing object at that key.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: The backend first authorizes the business operation, chooses an object key, and signs a short-lived operation. The client uses that capability to send bytes directly to object storage, removing the application server from the bulk-data path.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: For a toy avatar upload, the server allocates users/42/uploads/random-id, returns an expiring upload capability, and records pending status. After upload, a validation step checks actual type and size before making the object public or marking it active.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: A presigned URL is a bearer capability. Anyone who obtains it can use its permitted operation before expiry, subject to the service’s conditions.
Control key choice, expiry, size or content restrictions supported by the selected upload mechanism, and overwrite behavior.
Authorization to upload is not evidence that uploaded content is safe or that the upload finished.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: How do you prevent a client from overwriting another user’s object, and how does the application confirm and validate completion?

guides.title: A cache key is a response-sharing contract
guides.summary: Values that determine which response is safe to reuse, such as the path and relevant query, language, or tenant variants. Omitting a meaningful variant can return the wrong content; including irrelevant high-cardinality values fragments the cache. Forward analytics-only values separately. Sensitive personalized responses may need caching disabled rather than a shared cache entry.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Values that determine which response is safe to reuse, such as the path and relevant query, language, or tenant variants. Omitting a meaningful variant can return the wrong content; including irrelevant high-cardinality values fragments the cache. Forward analytics-only values separately. Sensitive personalized responses may need caching disabled rather than a shared cache entry.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A shared cache can reuse a response only when every caller mapped to its key may safely receive that response. Include the request dimensions that actually change the representation, while avoiding irrelevant high-cardinality values that destroy reuse.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: GET /prices varies by currency. If the key ignores currency, a EUR request may reuse a USD response. If the key includes a unique analytics trace ID, almost every request misses. Forward analytics data independently where the platform permits.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: For tenant- or user-specific content, isolation is a correctness and security requirement. Sometimes the correct answer is no shared caching.
Align origin variation, cache-key policy, and response cache headers.
Test two users with different privileges and two representation variants against the same edge cache.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Write a pair of requests that must share a response and a pair that must never share. Does the key enforce both?

guides.title: Elasticsearch write acknowledgement versus search visibility
guides.summary: Search visibility depends on refresh. The default write path does not wait for the change to become searchable. If that write must be visible before replying, refresh=wait_for usually waits for a refresh; refresh=true forces one and adds indexing, search, and merge costs. Refresh visibility is a separate concern from transactional correctness across systems.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Search visibility depends on refresh. The default write path does not wait for the change to become searchable. If that write must be visible before replying, refresh=wait_for usually waits for a refresh; refresh=true forces one and adds indexing, search, and merge costs. Refresh visibility is a separate concern from transactional correctness across systems.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A successful indexing request and visibility in a search query are distinct milestones. Refresh exposes recent changes to search. Waiting for refresh can be useful for a read-after-write experience; forcing refresh repeatedly can add significant work.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy article editor saves a post and immediately searches for its unique title. The write succeeded, yet the search index has not refreshed. The UI can show the saved document directly or use an appropriate wait-for-refresh write path when the product truly needs immediate search visibility.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Prefer normal refresh behavior for bulk indexing throughput.
refresh=wait_for and refresh=true have different effects; do not force refresh on every write without measurement.
A search replica is often a derived view. Plan rebuilds and reconcile source-of-truth changes.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Would a direct read by ID satisfy the interaction, or does the user specifically need an updated search result set?

guides.title: A timeout means an unknown outcome
guides.summary: No. The server may have committed before the response was lost. Query by a stable operation ID or retry using the same ID if the API provides an idempotency contract. Generating a new ID can create a second order. Without such a contract, reconcile the uncertain outcome before repeating a non-idempotent action.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. The server may have committed before the response was lost. Query by a stable operation ID or retry using the same ID if the API provides an idempotency contract. Generating a new ID can create a second order. Without such a contract, reconcile the uncertain outcome before repeating a non-idempotent action.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Transport failure describes what the client observed, not whether the server changed state. The server may finish the operation while the response is delayed or lost. A repeated non-idempotent request can create a second effect.

sections.title: Worked scenario

guides.title: 12 · Deadlocks and starvation
guides.summary: Thread A holds lock X while waiting for Y; thread B holds Y while waiting for X. Neither can progress. A consistent global lock acquisition order prevents that cycle. Short critical sections, limited nesting, and avoiding blocking waits make the system easier to reason about.

sections.title: Recall target

sections.title: Mental model
