guides.title: 02 · SELECT, expressions, and aliases
guides.summary: SELECT chooses the output columns and expressions. WHERE decides which source rows survive. AS names an output expression. Listing required columns makes the result contract clearer than SELECT *.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: SELECT chooses the output columns and expressions. WHERE decides which source rows survive. AS names an output expression. Listing required columns makes the result contract clearer than SELECT *.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Read a simple query as FROM the source, WHERE eligible rows, SELECT output expressions, ORDER BY the final sequence. That is a useful logical model, not a promise about the physical execution order. Expressions run per output row unless aggregation changes the grain.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT order_id, total_cents, total_cents / 100.0 AS total_units
FROM Orders
WHERE order_id IN (101, 102)
ORDER BY order_id;

sections.title: Expected result on the shared toy data
sections.code:
order_id | total_cents | total_units
101 | 1200 | 12.0
102 | 800 | 8.0

sections.title: Read the result
paragraphs: Only orders 101 and 102 survive. The result keeps cents and adds a display-oriented division. The .0 avoids integer division in these engines; production monetary formatting and precision deserve an explicit type and rounding policy.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: An alias changes the result label, not the stored column.
Do not rely on a SELECT alias in WHERE in SQL Server; repeat the expression or use a subquery/CTE.
SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate complete result rows, not duplicate values in just one arbitrarily chosen column.

guides.title: 03 · WHERE, AND/OR, IN, ranges, and LIKE
guides.summary: AND binds more tightly than OR. Parentheses state the intended grouping and make review safer. WHERE retains only rows whose predicate is TRUE; FALSE and UNKNOWN do not pass.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: AND binds more tightly than OR. Parentheses state the intended grouping and make review safer. WHERE retains only rows whose predicate is TRUE; FALSE and UNKNOWN do not pass.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Predicates compare values or combine conditions. IN is useful for a small membership list. BETWEEN includes both endpoints. LIKE uses % for any-length text and _ for one character; case behavior depends on database collation and settings. For dates with time components, prefer a half-open range.

sections.title: Worked query

SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_cents
FROM Orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND (customer_id = 1 OR total_cents >= 2000)
ORDER BY order_id;

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Use = for SQL equality, not == when writing portable SQL.
A leading wildcard like %book can make a conventional prefix index less useful.
A filter on a timestamp ending at midnight can omit the rest of that calendar day.

guides.title: 04 · ORDER BY, ties, and limiting rows
guides.summary: Limiting rows does not define which rows come first. Use ORDER BY for the intended order and a unique tie-breaker for deterministic results. SQL Server uses TOP or OFFSET/FETCH; SQLite uses LIMIT.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: Limiting rows does not define which rows come first. Use ORDER BY for the intended order and a unique tie-breaker for deterministic results. SQL Server uses TOP or OFFSET/FETCH; SQLite uses LIMIT.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: ASC sorts ascending and DESC descending. Multiple expressions are compared from left to right. If two rows tie on every ordering expression, their relative order is not guaranteed. Selecting the newest items therefore often uses a timestamp plus a unique ID.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT order_id, ordered_on
FROM Orders
ORDER BY ordered_on DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 2;

sections.title: Expected result on the shared toy data
Read the result
paragraphs: Orders 105 and 106 share a date. Descending order_id puts 106 first consistently. LIMIT is shown only in the executed SQLite version; the equivalent SQL Server example is below.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Do not depend on insertion order, index order, or yesterday’s query result order.
TOP WITH TIES can return more than the requested count; use it only when that is the desired meaning.
Sort direction applies per expression, so write DESC on each intended descending key.

guides.title: 05 · NULL and three-valued logic
guides.summary: Comparisons with NULL produce UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE. WHERE keeps only TRUE. Test missing values with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; use COALESCE only when a replacement matches the business meaning.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: Comparisons with NULL produce UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE. WHERE keeps only TRUE. Test missing values with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; use COALESCE only when a replacement matches the business meaning.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: SQL’s third truth value matters: TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN; FALSE AND UNKNOWN is FALSE; TRUE OR UNKNOWN is TRUE. Missing data is not an ordinary value that can be compared using = NULL. Likewise, NOT IN can behave unexpectedly if its list or subquery contains NULL.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT customer_id, name, COALESCE(city, '(unknown)') AS city_label
FROM Customers
WHERE city <> 'Oslo' OR city IS NULL
ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.code:

2 | Ben | Paris
3 | Cy | (unknown)

sections.title: Read the result

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: city = NULL matches no rows under standard NULL semantics.
COUNT(city) excludes NULL while COUNT(*) counts rows.
Replacing unknown money with zero can invent a fact; COALESCE is a semantic choice.

guides.title: 06 · COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX
guides.summary: COUNT(*) counts result rows. COUNT(column) counts rows where that expression is not NULL. SUM and AVG generally ignore NULL inputs; an empty qualifying set yields NULL for SUM and AVG but zero for COUNT.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: COUNT(*) counts result rows. COUNT(column) counts rows where that expression is not NULL. SUM and AVG generally ignore NULL inputs; an empty qualifying set yields NULL for SUM and AVG but zero for COUNT.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: An aggregate combines several input rows into one result value. First decide the grain: here the source is one row per order. Join multiplication can change the rows being aggregated, so a correct-looking SUM can still answer the wrong question.

sections.title: Worked query

SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(total_cents) AS total_cents,
       AVG(total_cents * 1.0) AS average_cents,
       MIN(total_cents) AS smallest, MAX(total_cents) AS largest
FROM Orders;

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Do not average averages across differently sized groups; retain group counts or underlying totals.
SUM(DISTINCT amount) removes repeated amounts, not duplicate business records.
For no orders, decide whether the interface should show NULL or zero and apply COALESCE deliberately.

guides.title: 07 · GROUP BY and HAVING
guides.summary: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. GROUP BY defines one result row per grouping key. HAVING filters the resulting groups, often using an aggregate. SELECT nonaggregated columns must be compatible with the grouping rules.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. GROUP BY defines one result row per grouping key. HAVING filters the resulting groups, often using an aggregate. SELECT nonaggregated columns must be compatible with the grouping rules.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Think in two grains: input order rows and output customer groups. Filtering pending orders before grouping changes the totals. Filtering groups after aggregation asks which customers meet a total-based condition. These are different operations.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS paid_orders, SUM(total_cents) AS paid_cents
FROM Orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total_cents) >= 2500
ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.title: Expected result on the shared toy data
sections.code:
customer_id | paid_orders | paid_cents
2 | 2 | 3200

sections.title: Read the result
paragraphs: After the paid filter, Ada’s two orders total 2400 and Ben’s two total 3200. HAVING keeps only Ben’s group. Cy has no paid input rows, and Dee has no orders at all; neither group exists in this query.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Grouping does not automatically sort the result.
SQL Server does not allow an arbitrary ungrouped name beside customer_id and SUM; group or join appropriately.
A WHERE total_cents >= 2500 would filter individual orders, producing a different answer.

guides.title: 08 · INNER JOIN and matching rows
guides.summary: It produces one result row for each matching customer-order pair, so that customer appears three times. A join combines related rows; it does not automatically return one row per entity or remove duplicates.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: It produces one result row for each matching customer-order pair, so that customer appears three times. A join combines related rows; it does not automatically return one row per entity or remove duplicates.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Use an explicit join condition that represents the relationship. Qualify columns with table aliases to make ownership clear. A missing or incorrect relationship can create far more pairs than intended. Start by stating the output grain: one row per order here.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.total_cents
FROM Orders AS o
INNER JOIN Customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id <= 103
ORDER BY o.order_id;

102 | Ada | 800
103 | Ben | 2000

sections.title: Read the result
paragraphs: Orders 101 and 102 both link to customer 1, so Ada appears twice. Every order in this fixture has a valid customer because the foreign key protects the reference. An inner join would omit unmatched rows if the relationship were optional or unenforced.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Join on stable keys, not names that can repeat or change.
Two tables having an id column does not mean those IDs represent the same thing.
Adding DISTINCT to hide unexpected duplicates often conceals an incorrect join.

guides.title: 09 · LEFT JOIN, missing matches, and filter placement
guides.summary: LEFT JOIN supplies NULL right-side columns for unmatched left rows. A right-side comparison in WHERE often rejects those NULL rows. Put a matching-condition filter in ON when the left rows must remain even without qualifying matches.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: LEFT JOIN supplies NULL right-side columns for unmatched left rows. A right-side comparison in WHERE often rejects those NULL rows. Put a matching-condition filter in ON when the left rows must remain even without qualifying matches.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: A left join preserves each left row and adds all qualifying right matches. To count optional children, count the child’s non-null key rather than COUNT(*), because an unmatched left row still produces one null-extended result row.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS paid_orders
FROM Customers AS c
LEFT JOIN Orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

sections.title: Expected result on the shared toy data

1 | Ada | 2
2 | Ben | 2
3 | Cy | 0
4 | Dee | 0

sections.title: Read the result
paragraphs: Cy’s canceled order does not qualify in ON, but Cy remains with no paid match. Dee also remains. COUNT(o.order_id) is zero for both. COUNT(*) would misleadingly count their null-extended rows as one.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: WHERE o.status = 'paid' after this left join would remove Cy and Dee.
Testing a nullable business column for absence can be misleading; test the non-null child key.
Multiple matching children still multiply rows, even in a left join.

guides.title: 10 · Join multiplicity and avoiding double counting
guides.summary: The order’s total repeats once per matching line. Summing at that expanded grain counts some orders more than once. Aggregate at the intended grain before joining, or sum line amounts when that is the actual measure.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: The order’s total repeats once per matching line. Summing at that expanded grain counts some orders more than once. Aggregate at the intended grain before joining, or sum line amounts when that is the actual measure.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Name the grain of every intermediate result. Orders is one row per order; the order-to-line join is one row per line. When joining two one-to-many child sets, the result can multiply both sides. DISTINCT amounts are not a repair because separate orders can legitimately have identical totals.

sections.title: Worked query

SELECT o.order_id, o.total_cents,
       SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_cents) AS line_total_cents
FROM Orders AS o
JOIN OrderItems AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id, o.total_cents
ORDER BY o.order_id;

Read the result
paragraphs: Grouping restores one row per order and sums each line’s actual contribution. On the raw join, SUM(o.total_cents) would be 10800 instead of 7200 because orders 101, 105, and 106 each have two lines.

bullets: COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) can count unique orders, but it does not fix unrelated sum expressions.
SUM(DISTINCT total_cents) would collapse legitimate orders with the same amount.
Preaggregate each child table separately before joining multiple child totals to a parent.

guides.title: 11 · Subqueries, EXISTS, and NOT EXISTS
guides.summary: Use EXISTS when you only need to know whether at least one related row exists. It preserves the outer query’s grain without emitting one row per match. NOT EXISTS asks whether no qualifying match exists and avoids the NULL trap of many NOT IN expressions.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: Use EXISTS when you only need to know whether at least one related row exists. It preserves the outer query’s grain without emitting one row per match. NOT EXISTS asks whether no qualifying match exists and avoids the NULL trap of many NOT IN expressions.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: A subquery is a query nested in another statement. A correlated subquery refers to the current outer row. SQL describes the relationship logically; the optimizer can choose an efficient physical plan rather than literally executing the subquery as written for every row.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM Customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM Orders AS o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

1 | Ada
2 | Ben

sections.title: Read the result
paragraphs: Ada and Ben each have qualifying orders but appear only once. The SELECT 1 inside EXISTS is a conventional marker; the existence of rows is what matters. NOT EXISTS with the same predicate would return Cy and Dee.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: A scalar subquery used as one value must produce at most one row; multiple matches can be an error.
NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery may make every comparison UNKNOWN.
Do not assume every correlated query is slow; inspect the actual plan and data.

guides.title: 12 · CTEs: name an intermediate result
guides.summary: No. A CTE names a query expression for the immediately following statement. It improves structure and readability; materialization and repeated work depend on the engine and plan. Use a temporary table when you specifically need stored intermediate results and accept its costs.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: No. A CTE names a query expression for the immediately following statement. It improves structure and readability; materialization and repeated work depend on the engine and plan. Use a temporary table when you specifically need stored intermediate results and accept its costs.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Break a complex question into grains. First calculate totals per customer, then join names and filter. A CTE helps make these transformations visible. In SQL Server, terminate the preceding statement before WITH; starting with ;WITH is a common safe convention.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
WITH Totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_cents) AS cents
  FROM Orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, t.cents
FROM Totals AS t
JOIN Customers AS c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.cents >= 3000
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Ada | 3200
Ben | 3200

bullets: A CTE lasts one statement, not the whole connection.
A CTE is not inherently faster than a subquery with the same logic.

guides.title: 13 · CASE and conditional aggregation
guides.summary: Use a conditional expression inside an aggregate, for example SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). CASE chooses a value; it is an expression, not a general procedural control-flow block.

paragraphs: Use a conditional expression inside an aggregate, for example SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). CASE chooses a value; it is an expression, not a general procedural control-flow block.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: CASE turns a condition into a result value for each input row. Aggregation can then combine those values. Be explicit about ELSE: without it, unmatched rows produce NULL, which changes how aggregates count or sum them.

  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending_count
FROM Orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

guides.summary: Assign ROW_NUMBER over each customer partition ordered by date descending and a unique ID descending, then keep rn = 1 in an outer query. GROUP BY with MAX(date) alone does not identify every other column from the latest row.

guides.title: 15 · Running totals and explicit window frames
guides.summary: It explicitly sums from the first row through the current row in the window’s sequence. A deterministic order plus a ROWS frame gives row-by-row accumulation. Default frames and peer rows can produce surprising totals when ordering values tie.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: It explicitly sums from the first row through the current row in the window’s sequence. A deterministic order plus a ROWS frame gives row-by-row accumulation. Default frames and peer rows can produce surprising totals when ordering values tie.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: A window aggregate preserves each input row and adds a calculation over a frame. PARTITION BY restarts the total for each customer. ORDER BY defines progression. The frame tells the engine which preceding, current, or following rows contribute.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT order_id, total_cents,
  SUM(total_cents) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id
    ORDER BY ordered_on, order_id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_cents
FROM Orders
WHERE customer_id = 1
ORDER BY ordered_on, order_id;

102 | 800 | 2000

bullets: Do not confuse the window frame with the entire partition.
Filter placement changes which rows enter the window; an outer filter can preserve a total computed over more rows.
Use a stable tie-breaker so equal dates do not leave the sequence ambiguous.

guides.summary: It enforces that a non-null referencing value matches an allowed parent key. It does not automatically mean one-to-one, create every helpful index, or enforce unrelated business rules. Nullability and uniqueness define additional parts of the relationship.

guides.title: 23 · Database deadlocks and safe retries
guides.summary: Blocking can resolve when the owner releases a resource. A deadlock is a cycle: each participant waits for a resource held by another in the cycle. SQL Server can choose a victim and roll it back. Retry the whole transaction with bounded backoff when safe.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: Blocking can resolve when the owner releases a resource. A deadlock is a cycle: each participant waits for a resource held by another in the cycle. SQL Server can choose a victim and roll it back. Retry the whole transaction with bounded backoff when safe.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Prevent common cycles with consistent resource ordering, short transactions, and appropriate indexes that reduce unnecessary locking. Diagnose the actual deadlock graph rather than assuming every timeout is a deadlock. Isolation and access plans affect which resources are locked.

guides.title: 24 · Offset versus keyset pagination
guides.summary: It stores the last seen ordering values, then asks for rows after that position. A unique tie-breaker makes the order total, so equal timestamps do not create ambiguous page boundaries. Offset skips a count of rows and can become costly or shift under concurrent changes.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: It stores the last seen ordering values, then asks for rows after that position. A unique tie-breaker makes the order total, so equal timestamps do not create ambiguous page boundaries. Offset skips a count of rows and can become costly or shift under concurrent changes.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: For descending (ordered_on, order_id), the next page has an earlier date or the same date with a smaller ID. Match the comparison direction to the sort. Use an opaque validated cursor in an API, keep filters stable, and consider snapshot semantics if a consistent whole-list traversal matters.

FROM Orders
WHERE ordered_on < '2026-02-02'

ORDER BY ordered_on DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 2;

Read the result

bullets: Keyset pagination is not automatic snapshot isolation; edits to sort keys can still affect traversal.

guides.summary: UNION combines compatible result sets and removes duplicate complete rows. UNION ALL keeps duplicates and avoids that deduplication requirement. Use ALL when duplicates are meaningful or the inputs are known to be disjoint.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: A join combines columns through related row pairs. A union stacks rows from separate queries with compatible column counts and types. The first query supplies result column names. Add final ordering to the combined result rather than assuming each input’s order is preserved.

guides.title: Consistency models and CAP without slogans
guides.summary: During a network partition, a distributed system cannot guarantee both linearizable operations and a successful response to every request at every non-failing node. State the operation and failure conditions rather than saying “pick any two”.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: During a network partition, a distributed system cannot guarantee both linearizable operations and a successful response to every request at every non-failing node. State the operation and failure conditions rather than saying “pick any two”.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Linearizability treats each operation as taking effect at one point between invocation and response, respecting completed-operation order. Eventual consistency permits temporary divergence with convergence under suitable conditions. Session guarantees such as read-your-writes are narrower and often useful. CAP consistency is not the C in ACID.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Two disconnected regions each have the last remaining toy ticket. Accepting sales independently risks overselling. Refusing or deferring the sale on a side that cannot establish authority sacrifices availability for that operation. A public catalog description can tolerate a different choice from ticket purchase.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: Availability in CAP is a formal response guarantee, not a monthly uptime percentage.
Healthy-network latency and consistency tradeoffs still exist; CAP does not choose your ordinary read strategy.
Define conflict resolution, authority, and recovery after connectivity returns.

guides.title: Rate limiting, token buckets, and admission control
guides.summary: A rate limit bounds work admitted over time. A concurrency limit bounds work in flight. Both may be needed because slow requests can occupy resources even at a modest arrival rate.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: A rate limit bounds work admitted over time. A concurrency limit bounds work in flight. Both may be needed because slow requests can occupy resources even at a modest arrival rate.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: A token bucket replenishes tokens at a set rate up to a capacity. An operation spends tokens; a full bucket permits a bounded burst. Fixed windows are simple but allow boundary bursts. Sliding approaches improve smoothness with additional state or approximation. Choose the key by the intended fairness unit, such as tenant or API credential.

sections.title: Worked scenario

If each request holds a database connection for five seconds, that rate can still create too many concurrent connections, so add a separate concurrency gate.

bullets: A per-process limiter’s total allowance grows when the fleet grows unless coordinated or allocated.
Decide fail-open versus fail-closed behavior for limiter-store failure based on the endpoint’s consequences.
Reject clearly, bound queues, and prevent retries from immediately undoing the protection.

guides.title: Load balancing, health checks, and stateless services
guides.summary: A load balancer routes traffic across targets. It can improve distribution and failure handling, but it does not make shared dependencies scale or turn local session state into durable shared state.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: A load balancer routes traffic across targets. It can improve distribution and failure handling, but it does not make shared dependencies scale or turn local session state into durable shared state.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Layer-4 routing operates around transport connections; layer-7 routing understands application protocol properties such as HTTP paths and headers. Health checks select eligible targets, while connection draining lets ongoing work finish during removal. Long-lived connections and uneven request costs complicate simple round-robin assumptions.

sections.title: Worked scenario

Store sessions appropriately or use a deliberate verifiable stateless token contract. Sticky routing can hide the problem until that instance fails.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: Separate liveness from readiness so starting or overloaded instances are not given work they cannot serve.
A database can remain the bottleneck after adding application replicas.
Keep enough spare capacity for one target to fail and test reconnect behavior for long-lived clients.

guides.title: Data modeling from access patterns and invariants
guides.summary: Choose a data model by the facts that must remain correct and the operations that must be efficient. A product label such as SQL or NoSQL is not a substitute for keys, queries, constraints, and a consistency contract.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: Choose a data model by the facts that must remain correct and the operations that must be efficient. A product label such as SQL or NoSQL is not a substitute for keys, queries, constraints, and a consistency contract.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Start with entities and their relationships, then list important reads and writes. Normalize changing facts to avoid accidental duplication. Denormalized or derived views can make reads cheap, but require an update and reconciliation strategy. Decide what is authoritative and what can be rebuilt.

guides.summary: Choose the simplest delivery mechanism that meets update frequency and direction needs. Polling is straightforward, SSE streams server-to-client events, and WebSockets support bidirectional messaging. The connection alone is not durable event delivery.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: Choose the simplest delivery mechanism that meets update frequency and direction needs. Polling is straightforward, SSE streams server-to-client events, and WebSockets support bidirectional messaging. The connection alone is not durable event delivery.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Persistent connections require lifecycle management: authentication, idle timeouts, heartbeats, reconnect backoff, per-client buffers, and slow-consumer policy. Server-side producers must route updates to the process holding the appropriate connection. Durable state and replay or resynchronization handle disconnections.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy export-progress page can poll every few seconds or receive one-way SSE status updates. A collaborative editor has frequent bidirectional interaction and may use WebSockets. In either case, reconnecting after missing updates needs a version or cursor, or a fresh authoritative snapshot.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: Do not buffer unlimited events for a disconnected or slow client.
A connected socket does not imply a user processed an event. Add application acknowledgements only when the contract needs them.
WebSocket delivery does not solve concurrent document-edit conflict resolution; that is a separate model.
